title: I went ghost-hunting, so I asked a paranormal investigator what equipment to buy
byline: Marie LodiFollowSenior Writer, Beauty Wed, October 28, 2026 at 5:15 PM UTCAdd to Preferred Sources
excerpt: Who you gonna call? Grab some $12 dowsing rods from Amazon and get to work — just remember that your intuition is free.
content:
If I weren't a beauty editor, I'd be a paranormal investigator. Ever since I was a kid, I've been obsessed with ghosts, cryptids, UFOs, psychic phenomena and other unexplainable mysteries. I seek out all things spooky any chance I get.

Earlier this month, my husband and I booked a night aboard one of what's supposedly the most haunted places on the planet: the Queen Mary in Long Beach, Calif. This wasn't my first ghost hunt, but it was the first time I came armed with equipment. So, along with my usual sheet masks and serums, plus a nautical-style vintage outfit (I must always dress in theme), I packed my dowsing rods (not to find water, but communicate with ghosts).

But I also wanted tips from a real professional, so I reached out to Sapphire Sandalo, a paranormal researcher, filmmaker, occultist and podcast host based in Los Angeles. Her first piece of advice might be surprising for a shopping story, but it makes sense. "I am a firm believer that your body is the No. 1 tool that you need on an investigation," she says. That means your intuition, your sense of discernment and your relationship with the spirit world. 

Still, she's not anti-gear — she just doesn't rely on it. "Things should be happening in tandem with what you're also feeling," she says. "So if someone's like, 'I'm feeling a sensation that something's here,' and then a thing goes off, it's reaffirming what you're feeling."

What to know before you go looking for ghosts

Before any gear comes out, Sandalo casts a protective circle in Cebuano, her family's Filipino language, and closes it at the end. "You're intentionally opening the door and then closing the door," she says. "It's not difficult to protect yourself." (My own Queen Mary ritual was some holy water, a Florida Water soap and a few protection words that sternly told the spirits onboard they were staying on the ship and not coming home with me.)

As for any ghost hunting apps, she's skeptical. "I don't know if they're intentionally putting out really creepy words so that you get scared," she says. Still, your phone is worth bringing to record photos and video, because sometimes the strangest moments show up on everyday devices. Case in point: Sandalo's best evidence ever was captured on a Zoom call.

Spoiler alert: I didn't see an actual ghost on the Queen Mary, though I did feel a heaviness and unease in certain parts of the ship — the submerged propeller is especially freaky. And I woke up at 4 a.m. to someone poking my shoulder hard. After a minute of pure terror, I deduced it was just my husband tossing and turning, but I still couldn't go back to sleep after that. The ship has plenty of rooms with reported hauntings, including the infamous stateroom B340, but ours seemed perfectly fine. Unfortunately.

Expert-recommended ghost-hunting equipment

So what's actually in a paranormal investigator's kit? Here's the gear Sandalo swears by, the gadgets she side-eyes and what to buy if you want to try a little ghost hunting yourself.

Sandalo's friend gave her a set of these letter dice, and now they’re a staple. During an investigation at the Glen Tavern Inn in Santa Paula, Calif., the name "Kane" came up every time she tossed them. "We were like, 'Kane’s here,'" she laughs.

These were the first things to go in my suitcase. People have used dowsing rods for centuries to find water, but some ghost hunters use them to ask yes-or-no questions. You hold one loosely in each hand and ask a spirit to cross the rods for "yes" and open outward for "no." Skeptics chalk it up to tiny unconscious hand motions, known as the ideomotor effect. But at this price, they're a good way to start, and they look super chic on your bookshelf when you're not ghost-hunting. 

This is the meter I brought aboard the Queen Mary. It’s affordable; I’d used one on ghost tours before and it’s an easy way to dip a toe into ghost-hunting gear. The black paddle with rainbow LEDs was originally designed to detect electromagnetic fields from things like faulty wiring, so I knew going in that it could pick up interference. Sandalo confirms it. "Your phone will set it off," she says, and so will electrical outlets. 

Her rule for this and every other gadget: Cross off every rational explanation before you get excited. "If you have your meter and it's just sitting there and there's no other interference, and all of a sudden it's going real crazy after you ask it something, that's something to pay attention to," she says.

Sandalo keeps a separate tarot deck just for investigations. "I have a relationship with the cards, so it works for me," she says. While the group asks questions, she shuffles, and "sometimes a card will pop out, and it feels very relevant to the question that we asked." Her advice is to bring whatever divination tool you already click with. "I like the tangible, non-electronic equipment," she says. If you're new to tarot cards, this classic deck is an easy place to start.

A regular digital voice recorder is another one of the most accessible tools on this list. I already had one lying around for interviews, so after reading up on electronic voice phenomena, I tossed it in my bag. EVP research dates to 1959, when Swedish artist and filmmaker Friedrich Jürgenson heard what sounded like a human voice while playing back a tape recording. He blamed faulty equipment at first, but when he checked other tapes, he found more voices that seemed to be messages from his dead mother.

The catch to using one? Someone has to listen to all of it. (I may have eight hours of unreviewed audio from my night on the Queen Mary...)

The P-SB7 works by sweeping through radio frequencies, with the theory that spirits can speak through the static. "The boring, skeptical explanation is that it's just the pareidolia effect, where you're hearing bits and pieces of different radio stations, and obviously you're going to pick up on words every now and then," Sandalo says. "But I've been in situations where you hear something that you're like, there's no way that that was just an accident. It was way too pertinent." 

Her favorite way to use a spirit box is the Estes Method. It's named for Estes Park, Colo., where in 2016, investigators first developed the technique at the Stanley Hotel, the reportedly haunted hotel that inspired Stephen King's The Shining. One person wears a blindfold and noise-isolating headphones plugged into the spirit box and calls out whatever they hear while the other person asks questions. "You become the spirit box," Sandalo says. "You have to have a human element to the equipment that you're using, because the paranormal comes from people."

If you watch ghost-hunting shows, you've probably seen this cylinder-shaped object with a little antenna. It gives off its own electromagnetic field, then lights up and beeps when something enters that field. Some versions, like this one, also flag sudden temperature changes. Sandalo calls it "one of the basics every investigator will probably have" but warns it's easily triggered. "There are a lot of things that can set those off that are not paranormal-related, and the most common one is that if you press a walkie-talkie button nearby, it will go off," she explains, adding that she suspects some TV productions may use that trick on purpose.
